items.title: Creative destruction: Human-AI competition in an experimental market
items.desc: Three experiments (N = 1,025) have participants design computer games with an AI coding agent and then buy them; games designed by the AI alone outperform those by human producers, including professional creatives, and producers do not anticipate this. Telling consumers a game is human-designed does not raise willingness to pay. [arXiv econ.GN, submitted 2026-10-12]

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Today a paper asks whether humans keep a role in production as AI improves. This one is based on the abstract only.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Two ideas are tested: humans might have a durable edge in taste and design, or consumers might simply prefer human-made products.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: In the experiments, participants act as producers designing computer games with an AI coding agent, and as consumers who buy the games. Across three studies with about one thousand twenty-five participants, they find no evidence for either idea.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Games designed by the AI on its own did better than those from human producers, including amateurs and professional creatives.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Human producers also did not anticipate the AI's advantage.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: And revealing that a game was human designed did not raise what consumers were willing to pay.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: So the takeaway is that neither taste nor a human-made premium obviously protects human roles, at least in this market.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: A fair caveat is that it is an experimental market for games, so results may not carry over everywhere.

items.title: Recurrent Neural Networks for Forecasting Autoregressive Noncausal Processes
items.desc: Compares RNN, LSTM, GRU, bidirectional LSTM and feed-forward networks for forecasting extreme values of noncausal time series that mimic bubbles and spikes; the simple feed-forward network does best at predicting extremes during a bubble, with further gains from pooling and a modified loss function. [arXiv econ.EM, submitted 2026-10-11]

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: This paper uses neural networks to forecast bubbles in economic time series. It is based on the abstract only.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: The series are autoregressive causal-noncausal processes, which show local explosive patterns like bubbles and spikes.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: The authors compare recurrent networks, LSTMs, GRUs, a bidirectional LSTM and a simple feed-forward network, across different training set lengths.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Surprisingly, the simple feed-forward network is best at predicting extreme values of a noncausal series during a bubble.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: They also show that pooling forecasts and a modified loss function improve point predictions of extreme values.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: The takeaway: for bubble-like data, fancier architectures are not automatically better.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Let me add some context on why anyone cares about noncausal processes. In economics, these models are used to capture episodes where a series climbs sharply and then crashes, which is how many people describe asset bubbles and commodity price spikes. Forecasting the peak is notoriously difficult, because the pattern looks locally explosive.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: That is why the question here is specifically about extreme values, not average accuracy. The authors vary both the type of network and the length of the training set, to see how each choice affects the ability to call those extremes during a bubble.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: The headline is that the plain feed-forward network outperforms the recurrent variants, including LSTM, GRU and bidirectional LSTM, when predicting extreme values of a univariate noncausal series during a bubble. They also report that pooling predictions and using a modified loss function improve the point predictions of extremes.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Remember we are working only from the abstract, so details like exact error figures are not covered here. Still, the practical message for forecasters is to test simple networks before reaching for complex ones.

items.title: Data-Driven Dynamic Portfolio Selection with Vine Copula Simulation and Reinforcement Learning
items.desc: Combines vine-copula scenario simulation with a recurrent reinforcement-learning policy for a CRRA investor with a CVaR penalty, with error bounds; on a seven-asset panel of US and Chinese equities and gold, an ensemble of ten policies reaches a 34.13% CAGR and Sharpe ratio of 2.31 over 22 monthly periods, beating six benchmarks. [arXiv q-fin.PM, submitted 2026-10-14]

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Here is a q-fin paper on portfolio choice with reinforcement learning, based on the abstract only.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: The investor has constant relative risk aversion and maximizes expected terminal utility, with a penalty on conditional value at risk.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: The method estimates a vine copula model from historical returns, then uses it to simulate scenarios and train a recurrent portfolio policy.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: The authors also derive bounds showing how errors in the fitted model carry through to policy values.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: On seven assets, US and Chinese equities and gold, an ensemble of ten policies earns a compound annual growth rate of thirty-four point one three percent and a Sharpe ratio of two point three one over twenty-two monthly periods, ahead of six benchmarks.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Mixing simulated with historical training data cut monthly turnover by forty-one point five percent with comparable growth.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: The caveat is a short evaluation window of twenty-two months, so treat the headline numbers carefully.

items.title: Beyond Time Induction: Structured Conditional Neural Solvers for Parametric Stochastic-Volatility Pricing
items.desc: Introduces BeTINN, a physics-informed neural architecture for solving the parametric Heston stochastic-volatility PDE, improving joint accuracy of option values and sensitivities over baselines and showing that low validation loss does not guarantee accurate derivatives. [arXiv cs.LG, submitted 2026-10-13]

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: This paper uses neural networks to price options. It is based on the abstract only.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Physics-informed neural networks can learn families of PDE solutions without labeled data, but keeping derivatives accurate across regimes is hard.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: The authors introduce BeTINN, which conditions on both time and model parameters and adds a joint residual pathway.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: They test it on the Heston stochastic volatility PDE, where sensitivities like the Greeks matter economically, and report better joint accuracy on option values and key sensitivities than their baselines.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: An important finding is that low validation physics loss does not fully determine derivative accuracy, so evaluation should check sensitivities directly.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: To put this in context, the Heston model is a standard stochastic volatility setup in options pricing, and its pricing equation is a partial differential equation with mixed derivatives. Traders care not only about the option value but also about sensitivities, which are the first and second order derivatives of that value.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: The authors' neural architecture, BeTINN, extends an earlier idea called time induced modulation. It conditions the network on both time and the model parameters in several directions, and adds a joint residual pathway, so one network can cover a whole family of parameter settings.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: They run controlled ablations to see which architectural pieces matter, and report improved joint accuracy across normalized option value and key sensitivity metrics relative to their baselines.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: The caution flagged in the abstract is that accurate solution values can coexist with localized derivative errors. So a model can look good on price and still be off on sensitivities, which are what hedging depends on. Again, this summary rests on the abstract alone.

items.title: Enhancing credit risk scorecards with transactional-based behavioural features
items.desc: Uses natural language processing and a RegEx-based categorisation algorithm to turn raw transaction narratives from a South African SME lender into behavioural features; adding them to a credit scorecard significantly raises the Gini. [arXiv q-fin.RM, submitted 2026-10-09]

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: This paper mines bank transaction text for credit scoring, based on the abstract only.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Using data from a large South African lender focused on small businesses, the authors apply language processing and regular expressions to categorize payment narratives into interpretable spending categories.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: The categorization algorithm shows high accuracy, and adding the features to a traditional scorecard significantly increases the Gini.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: The takeaway is that unstructured transaction text can improve credit models while staying explainable.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: A little more on the setup. Credit scorecards normally rely on credit history, repayment behavior, income and outstanding debt. Transaction data is sometimes added through summary measures like recency, frequency and monetary value, but the free text describing each payment has mostly gone unused because it is messy and unstructured.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: The authors work with data from a large South African financial institution focused on small and medium enterprises. They develop a novel categorization algorithm, combining language processing with regular expressions, that sorts transaction descriptions into interpretable spending categories. They then evaluate its classification accuracy, which they describe as high.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: The categories become behavioral features that are added to a credit risk scorecard. The result is a significant increase in the Gini coefficient compared with a scorecard without them.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: The authors stress explainability, which matters in lending, because the features are readable categories rather than opaque model outputs. As before, we only have the abstract, so we cannot say how large the Gini gain is.

sections.name: 📦 Operations & Supply Chain (INFORMS: Management Science, M&SOM, Operations Research)

items.title: AI-Driven Human Task Substitution: Evidence from Google Translate and ChatGPT
items.desc: Difference-in-differences on an online labor market for translation: Google Neural Machine Translation reduced demand for analytical tasks but not intuitive ones (transcreation), while ChatGPT cut demand substantially for both, so which work is resilient does not generalize from predictive to generative AI. [Management Science, published online 2026-10-14]

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: This Management Science paper studies how AI substitutes for knowledge work, based on the abstract only.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: It uses two natural experiments in an online translation labor market: Google Neural Machine Translation and then ChatGPT.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Regular translations count as analytical tasks, while transcreations needing creative and cultural adaptation count as intuitive tasks.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Google's system reduced demand for analytical tasks by meaningful amounts and had no detectable effect on intuitive ones.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: ChatGPT produced much larger and more uniform reductions in both kinds.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: So lessons about which jobs are safe from predictive AI do not carry over to generative AI.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Some detail on the design. The researchers estimate difference-in-differences models on transaction level data from an online labor market, using 2016 to 2017 for the Google neural translation episode and 2022 to 2023 for ChatGPT.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: They split work into analytical tasks, meaning regular translations, and intuitive tasks, meaning transcreations that require creative and cultural adaptation. The question is which kind of work a given generation of AI can replace.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: The finding for the earlier, task specific system is that it reduced demand for analytical tasks by economically meaningful magnitudes, with no detectable effect on intuitive tasks. For ChatGPT, the reductions were substantially larger and more uniform, hitting both kinds.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: The broader lesson is about the scope of substitution widening with generative AI. Conclusions about which human work is resilient, drawn from predictive AI, do not straightforwardly generalize. One caveat is that this is a single market, online translation, and we are working from the abstract only.
